title: ACA Section 1557 Nondiscrimination Final Rule (2024)
effective_date_notes: Rule effective 2024-07-05; some provisions have later compliance dates listed in 45 CFR 92.1 (for example 92.210(b)-(c) within 300 days). Provisions vacated to the extent they cover gender identity (Tennessee v. Kennedy, S.D. Miss., 2025-10-22; notice 91 FR 32887, 2026-06-02): 45 CFR 92.101(a)(2)(iv), 92.206(b)(1)-(4), 92.207(b)(3)-(5), 92.8(b)(1), 92.10(a)(1)(i), 92.208, and 42 CFR 438.3(d)(4), 438.206(c)(2), 440.262, 460.98(b)(3), 460.112(a).
triggers: An entity that receives HHS funding, runs a health program HHS administers, or is a Marketplace participant, and that uses health programs or technology that could discriminate (race, color, national origin, sex, age, disability).
example_tools: hospital patient-facing chatbot or portal; AI language-translation or interpreter tool used with patients; clinical risk score or triage algorithm used by a hospital or clinic; health plan prior-authorization or utilization-review model; machine-translated patient notices or discharge instructions; telehealth platform run by a Medicaid or Medicare provider
exclusions: Applies only to health programs or activities that receive Federal financial assistance from HHS (any part, directly or indirectly), are administered by HHS, or are administered by an ACA title I entity such as an Exchange (45 CFR 92.2(a)). Does not apply to an employer or other plan sponsor of a group health plan with regard to its employment practices, including employee health benefits (92.2(b)). A software vendor that receives no Federal financial assistance is not itself a covered entity; the duty falls on the covered entity that uses the tool. Gender-identity provisions listed in effective_date_notes are vacated (2026-06-02 notice).
key_definitions: 'Covered entity' = (1) a recipient of Federal financial assistance; (2) the Department (HHS); (3) an entity established under title I of the ACA (45 CFR 92.4); 'Federal financial assistance' = any grant, loan, credit, subsidy, contract (other than a procurement contract but including a contract of insurance) or other arrangement providing funds, federal personnel services, or property, and includes HHS payments, subsidies, or other funds extended to an entity providing health insurance coverage for a person's coverage, plus advance premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions (92.4); preamble: entities receiving Medicare Part C or Part D funding are recipients of Federal financial assistance (89 FR 37619-20), and HHS gave notice that Medicare Part B meets the definition (89 FR 37522, Section III); 'Health program or activity' = any project to provide or administer health-related services or coverage, help people obtain them, provide clinical, pharmaceutical, or medical care, engage in health or clinical research, or provide health education, plus all operations of an entity principally engaged in these (e.g. hospital, clinic, insurer, physician's practice, pharmacy) (92.4)
key_questions: Does the deploying organization receive any HHS funding (Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare Parts A, B, C, or D, HHS grants) or sell Marketplace plans?; Is the tool used in a health program or activity of that organization?; Does the tool communicate with patients or the public (accessibility and language access duties)?; Does it support clinical decisions about patients (see US-45CFR92.210)?; Is the developer itself a recipient of HHS funds, or only a vendor to one?
obligations: Do not discriminate in health programs, make information and communication technology accessible (92.204), take reasonable steps to give meaningful access to people with limited English proficiency (92.201), and follow the decision support tool rule (see US-45CFR92.210).
enforcement: HHS Office for Civil Rights enforces through complaints and compliance reviews using the Title VI, Title IX, Section 504, and Age Discrimination Act mechanisms (45 CFR 92.301), up to suspension or termination of federal funding (92.303). HHS says courts recognize a private right of action under Section 1557; the rule governs only OCR's administrative enforcement (89 FR 37522 preamble). The rule sets no damages or civil money penalties.
notes: Vacatur list read in the FR notice text; it states the other provisions remain in force. Sections 92.201, 92.204, 92.210 read in eCFR. Enforcement verified 2026-10-10 (92.301, 92.303, preamble).

title: Federal Wiretap Act: interception of communications and the one-party consent exception
citation: 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d); 18 U.S.C. 2510-2522 (Title III of Pub. L. 90-351, 82 Stat. 213; amended by Pub. L. 99-508)
effective_date_notes: One-party consent provision enacted 1968-06-19 as new 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) by Pub. L. 90-351, title III, sec. 802, 82 Stat. 213-214, covering 'wire or oral communication'. The Statutes at Large text for Title III shows no separate effective-date clause (searches for 'become effective' and 'take effect' found only the National Commission provision in sec. 804(k) and sec. 907 for Title IV firearms provisions), so effective on enactment is an inference. ECPA extended the exception to 'electronic communication': Pub. L. 99-508, title I, sec. 101(b)(2), Oct. 21, 1986, 100 Stat. 1849 (govinfo source credit; ECPA effective-date clause not checked). The 1968 text also ended with 'or for the purpose of committing any other injurious act'; the current text does not, and the date of that removal was not confirmed.
triggers: A tool records, transcribes, or otherwise captures the contents of a live conversation (phone or video call, or an in-person conversation where participants expect privacy) using a device or software, such as an ambient scribe, AI call recorder, or voice agent. Federal law allows it when the person recording is a party to the conversation or one party has given prior consent, unless the purpose is criminal or tortious.
example_tools: ambient scribe recording clinic visits; AI call recorder or call transcription for patient calls; AI voice agent answering or placing patient calls; telehealth video-visit recording and transcription; health plan call-center quality-assurance recorder
exclusions: The one-party consent exception in 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) covers a person 'not acting under color of law' who intercepts where that person is a party to the communication or one party has given prior consent, and it is lost if the interception is 'for the purpose of committing any criminal or tortious act in violation of the Constitution or laws of the United States or of any State'. It does not override stricter state all-party consent laws: for example California Penal Code 632 bars recording a confidential communication without the consent of all parties (632(a), text via FindLaw, tier 2). The federal text read does not itself state this preemption point; it is the requested framing and is not text-confirmed. Persons acting under color of law are governed by 2511(2)(c). Protection of 'oral communications' applies only where the speaker exhibits an expectation of non-interception that is justified by the circumstances (2510(2)). A device-based 'intercept' is the aural or other acquisition of contents through an electronic, mechanical, or other device (2510(4)).
key_definitions: 'Intercept' = 'the aural or other acquisition of the contents of any wire, electronic, or oral communication through the use of any electronic, mechanical, or other device' (2510(4)); 'wire communication' = 'any aural transfer made in whole or in part through the use of facilities for the transmission of communications by the aid of wire, cable, or other like connection' (2510(1)); 'oral communication' = 'any oral communication uttered by a person exhibiting an expectation that such communication is not subject to interception under circumstances justifying such expectation' (2510(2)); 'electronic communication' = any transfer of signs, signals, writing, images, sounds, data, or intelligence transmitted in whole or in part by a wire, radio, electromagnetic, photoelectronic, or photooptical system that affects interstate or foreign commerce (2510(12)); 'contents' = any information concerning the substance, purport, or meaning of the communication (2510(8)); one-party consent exception: 'It shall not be unlawful under this chapter for a person not acting under color of law to intercept a wire, oral, or electronic communication where such person is a party to the communication or where one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent to such interception unless such communication is intercepted for the purpose of committing any criminal or tortious act in violation of the Constitution or laws of the United States or of any State' (2511(2)(d)); California Penal Code 632: 'confidential communication' = any communication carried on in circumstances that may reasonably indicate a party desires it to be confined to the parties, excluding public gatherings and open legislative, judicial, or administrative proceedings (632(c), FindLaw)
key_questions: Is the person or system recording a party to the conversation, or has at least one participant given prior consent?; Where are the participants located, and does any involved state require all-party consent (e.g. California Penal Code 632 for confidential communications)?; Is the recording made for a criminal or tortious purpose?; Is the conversation a phone or video call (wire or electronic), or an in-person conversation where participants expect privacy (oral)?; Is the AI vendor itself a party to the conversation, or does it capture audio only through a participant who consented?; Has notice or consent been obtained from the patient and the clinician?
obligations: Do not intentionally intercept a wire, oral, or electronic communication, or use or disclose the contents of an unlawfully intercepted communication, unless an exception applies. A person not acting under color of law may intercept when that person is a party to the communication or one party has given prior consent, unless the interception is for the purpose of committing a criminal or tortious act (2511(1), (2)(d)).
enforcement: Criminal: fine or imprisonment up to five years, or both, for a violation of 2511(1) except as provided in (4)(b) and (5) (2511(4)(a); those carve-outs not read). Civil action under 18 U.S.C. 2520 by any person whose communication was intercepted, disclosed, or used: equitable or declaratory relief, damages (the greater of actual damages plus violator's profits, or statutory damages of the greater of $100 a day for each day of violation or $10,000), punitive damages in appropriate cases, and attorney's fees and costs (2520(a)-(c)(2)).
notes: Added in enrichment pass v0.3. Section 2511(2)(d) text, 2510 definitions, 2511(4)(a), and 2520 read on govinfo (U.S. Code 2023 edition); 1968 enactment text and date read in Pub. L. 90-351 (82 Stat. 197, govinfo STATUTE-82). California Penal Code 632 read via FindLaw (tier 2 mirror). The statement that the federal exception does not displace stricter state law is not stated in the federal text read; confirm against case law or legislative history before citing it as law. Not AI-specific; included because ambient scribes, call recorders, and voice agents capture conversations. Pending state-law litigation over AI recording vendors (e.g., under the California Invasion of Privacy Act) was not researched. Partially verified: effective date inferred from enactment, and the state-law interplay is not stated in the federal text.

title: Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records (Part 2)
effective_date_notes: Rule effective 2024-04-16; compliance date 2026-02-16 (FR DATES).
triggers: A federally assisted program holds substance use disorder treatment records, or a recipient of those records (including an AI vendor) uses or discloses them.
example_tools: AI documentation or ambient scribe used in an opioid treatment program or SUD clinic; predictive relapse or overdose-risk model trained on SUD treatment records; care-coordination platform that receives SUD treatment records from a Part 2 program; data analytics or population-health vendor serving a SUD treatment program (qualified service organization); chatbot for patients of a federally assisted addiction treatment program
exclusions: Covers only SUD information created by a Part 2 program; a patient record is not covered if the diagnosis, treatment, or referral was not provided by a federally assisted program (42 CFR 2.12(e)(1)-(2)). General medical facilities are covered only for an identified unit or staff that hold themselves out as providing SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral; e.g., emergency room personnel who refer an apparent overdose patient to the ICU are not covered unless their primary function is SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral and they are identified as such, or the ER has promoted itself as a provider of such services (2.12(e)(1)). A treating provider not subject to Part 2 may record SUD information, and doing so does not by itself make that provider's medical record subject to Part 2 (2.12(d)(2)(ii)). Not covered: a diagnosis made solely to provide evidence at the request of law enforcement or a court, and an overdose or intoxication diagnosis that clearly shows the person does not have a SUD (2.12(e)(4)). The use and disclosure restrictions do not apply to communications within a Part 2 program, or with an entity having direct administrative control over it, among personnel who need the information for SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral (2.12(c)(3)); to communications between a Part 2 program and a qualified service organization of information the QSO needs to provide services to the program (2.12(c)(4)), so a vendor with a QSO agreement can receive records for those services without patient consent but is bound by Part 2; to reports of crimes on program premises or against program personnel (2.12(c)(5)); or to state-law reports of suspected child abuse and neglect (2.12(c)(6)). VA records are governed by 38 U.S.C. 7332 instead (2.12(c)(1)).
key_definitions: 'Part 2 program' = a federally assisted program (2.11, 2.12(b)); 'Program' = (1) a person (other than a general medical facility) that holds itself out as providing, and provides, SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral for treatment; (2) an identified unit within a general medical facility that does so; or (3) medical personnel or staff in a general medical facility whose primary function is SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral and who are identified as such (2.11); 'Federally assisted' = conducted in whole or part by a federal agency; operating under a federal license, certification, registration, or other authorization (e.g. Medicare participating provider, authorization for maintenance treatment or withdrawal management, DEA registration to dispense controlled substances for SUD treatment); receiving federal financial assistance in any form, even if it does not directly pay for SUD services, or run by a state or local government unit receiving federal funds that could be spent on the program; or holding federal tax-exempt status or tax-deductible contributions (2.12(b)); 'Qualified service organization' = a person that (1) provides services to a Part 2 program, such as data processing, bill collecting, dosage preparation, laboratory analyses, legal, accounting, population health management, medical staffing, or other professional services, and (2) has a written agreement with the program acknowledging it is fully bound by Part 2 in dealing with patient records and will, if necessary, resist in judicial proceedings efforts to obtain access except as Part 2 permits; also includes a HIPAA business associate of a Part 2 program that is also a covered entity, for PHI that is also a Part 2 record (2.11); 'Patient identifying information' = name, address, Social Security number, fingerprints, photograph, or similar information by which a patient's identity can be determined with reasonable accuracy directly or by reference to other information (2.11)
key_questions: Does the customer hold itself out as providing SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral (or is it an identified SUD unit or staff in a general hospital)?; Is that customer federally assisted (Medicare participation, DEA registration for SUD treatment, federal funds, tax-exempt status)?; Does the tool receive, store, or analyze records that identify someone as having or having had a SUD, originating from that program?; Is the company a qualified service organization, business associate, or other lawful holder receiving Part 2 records?; Will Part 2 records be used for model training or redisclosed?; Is your own organization a federally assisted program that holds itself out as providing SUD diagnosis, treatment, or referral (the trigger rule doesn't capture this; if not, Part 2 reaches you only as a recipient of Part 2 records)?
obligations: Get patient consent before using or disclosing records (a single consent for all future treatment, payment, and health care operations is allowed), limit redisclosure, and keep security policies and breach notification procedures for records.
enforcement: Since the 2024 rule, Part 2 violations carry the HIPAA civil money penalty tiers and criminal penalties (42 U.S.C. 290dd-2(f), applying 1320d-5 and 1320d-6; 42 CFR 2.3(a)), with HHS enforcing under the HIPAA Enforcement Rule procedures (45 CFR part 160 subparts C-E, per 2.3(c)). 45 CFR 102.3 sets separate inflation-adjusted amounts for Part 2. Limited safe harbor for investigative agencies that acted with reasonable diligence (2.3(b)).
notes: Dates from FR DATES; consent and breach text read in eCFR 2.33 and 2.16. Verifier removed the de-identification clause (not checked in text). No later amendment found in FR search. Enforcement verified 2026-10-10 (290dd-2(f), 42 CFR 2.3).

title: Medicare Advantage coverage criteria and individualized determinations
effective_date_notes: CMS-4201-F effective 2023-06-05; provisions apply to coverage beginning 2024-01-01 (FR DATES). eCFR 422.101 later versions (2024-2026) not compared line by line; current text still contains the individualized-circumstances requirement.
triggers: A Medicare Advantage organization makes coverage or medical necessity decisions, including with algorithms or AI tools.
example_tools: Medicare Advantage prior-authorization review AI; post-acute care length-of-stay prediction tool used for coverage decisions; algorithmic medical-necessity screening for MA claims; automated denial or approval recommendation engine for an MA plan; internal coverage criteria engine or rules library
exclusions: Applies only to Medicare Advantage organizations (not traditional Medicare, Medicaid, or commercial plans). Internal coverage criteria may be used only when Medicare coverage criteria are not fully established (422.101(b)(6)). The text does not prohibit algorithms; it governs the basis for medical necessity decisions and who reviews adverse ones.
key_definitions: Medical necessity determinations must be based on coverage and benefit criteria in 422.101(b)-(c), whether the item or service is reasonable and necessary under section 1862(a)(1), the enrollee's medical history (e.g. diagnoses, conditions, functional status), physician recommendations, and clinical notes, and where appropriate the medical director (422.101(c)(1)(i)); 'Coverage criteria not fully established' = additional unspecified criteria are needed to interpret general provisions, NCDs or LCDs explicitly allow flexibility, or no applicable Medicare statute, regulation, NCD, or LCD sets criteria (422.101(b)(6)(i)); adverse medical necessity decisions must be reviewed by a physician or other appropriate health care professional with relevant expertise before issuance (422.566(d))
key_questions: Is the user a Medicare Advantage organization (or a vendor acting for one)?; Does the tool make or recommend coverage or medical necessity decisions?; Does it rely on criteria other than Medicare NCDs, LCDs, and publicly posted internal criteria?; Does it consider the individual enrollee's history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes?; Is every expected adverse decision reviewed by a qualified physician or professional before it issues?
obligations: Follow Traditional Medicare coverage criteria, use internal coverage criteria only when Medicare criteria are not fully established, base medical necessity decisions on the enrollee's medical history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes, and have a physician or other appropriate professional with relevant expertise review expected adverse medical necessity decisions (422.566(d)).
enforcement: CMS contract oversight, sanctions and corrective action plans.
notes: Citation 88 FR 22120 and dates confirmed in the FR API and DATES. Text of 422.101(c)(1)(i) and 422.566(d) read in eCFR. The rule does not name AI or algorithms; CMS applied it to AI in the FAQ memo.

title: Information Blocking Rule
effective_date_notes: Applicability date 2021-04-05 (moved from 2020-11-02 by interim final rule 85 FR 70064, 2020-11-04). Definition in 171.103 as amended by HTI-1 (89 FR 1436). HTI-5 proposes further information blocking changes.
trigger_rule: certified_developer OR certified_health_it OR hin_hie OR (org_provider AND health_info)
triggers: A health IT developer of certified health IT, health information network or exchange, or health care provider engages in a practice likely to interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information.
example_tools: EHR vendor AI add-on that restricts export of EHI; patient-access app or API integration; health system policy limiting third-party AI app access to patient data; HIE or data network serving AI developers; AI-generated clinical notes stored in the designated record set
exclusions: Applies only to three types of actors: health care providers, health IT developers of certified health IT, and health information networks or exchanges (45 CFR 171.102). A company that develops health IT but has no ONC-certified Health IT Module, and is not an HIN or HIE, is not an actor; a provider that self-develops health IT not offered to others is not a 'developer of certified health IT'. EHI excludes psychotherapy notes and information compiled for legal proceedings (171.102). Practices required by law or covered by an exception in Subparts B-D (e.g. privacy, security, infeasibility, preventing harm) are not information blocking.
key_definitions: 'Health IT developer of certified health IT' = an individual or entity, other than a health care provider that self-develops health IT not offered to others, that develops or offers health IT and that has, at the time of the practice, one or more Health IT Modules certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program (171.102); because the test is whether the entity holds any certified module, the definition is not limited on its face to practices involving the certified product (reading of the text, not an ONC statement checked); 'Health information network or health information exchange' = an entity that controls or administers policies or agreements enabling access, exchange, or use of EHI among more than two unaffiliated entities for treatment, payment, or operations (171.102); 'Electronic health information (EHI)' = ePHI to the extent it would be in a designated record set, whether or not held by a HIPAA covered entity, excluding psychotherapy notes and litigation material (171.102); 'Health care provider' = as defined in 42 U.S.C. 300jj (171.102)
key_questions: Does the company (or its parent) have any ONC-certified Health IT Module?; Does it run a network or exchange connecting more than two unaffiliated parties for treatment, payment, or operations?; Is the user a health care provider?; Does the practice limit access, exchange, or use of EHI (including AI outputs in the designated record set)?; Does an exception (privacy, security, infeasibility, preventing harm, content and manner) apply?
obligations: Do not engage in practices likely to interfere with access, exchange, or use of EHI unless required by law or an exception applies (for example, privacy, security, or infeasibility). Knowledge standard differs: developers and networks know or should know; providers know the practice is unreasonable.
enforcement: Developers of certified health IT and health information networks or exchanges: HHS OIG civil money penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation (42 U.S.C. 300jj-52(b)(2)(A); 42 CFR 1003.1410), for conduct on or after 2023-09-01. Health care providers face CMS disincentives instead (see US-ONC-INFOBLOCK-DISINCENTIVES-2024).
notes: 171.103 read in eCFR; applicability date from the 85 FR 70064 table. signed_or_published_date is the eCFR origin date (85 FR 25945, 2020-05-01). Statutory basis 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52 (eCFR authority). OIG penalty verified 2026-10-10 (300jj-52, 88 FR 42820). Verifier removed the unconfirmed 2022-10-06 EHI date.

title: Section 504 web content and mobile app accessibility
effective_date_notes: Rule effective 2024-07-08. Compliance moved by interim final rule 91 FR 25496 (published 2026-05-11, effective 2026-05-07, comments requested): recipients with 15 or more employees 2027-05-11 (was 2026-05-11); fewer than 15 employees 2028-05-10 (was 2027-05-10).
triggers: A recipient of HHS financial assistance (hospital, clinic, health system) provides web content or mobile apps, directly or through contracts, including patient-facing chatbots or portals.
example_tools: hospital website symptom checker or chatbot; patient portal with AI assistant; mobile health app provided by a health system; online appointment-scheduling bot; AI-generated patient education web pages
exclusions: Applies only to recipients of Federal financial assistance (45 CFR 84.10). Exceptions (84.85): archived web content; conventional electronic documents posted before the compliance date unless currently used to access programs; content posted by a third party unless posted under contract, license, or other arrangement with the recipient; individualized password-protected documents about a specific person or account; social media posts made before the compliance date. A recipient may show fundamental alteration or undue financial and administrative burden (84.84(b)).
key_definitions: 'Recipient' = any State or local government instrumentality, public or private agency, institution, organization, or person to which Federal financial assistance is extended directly or through another recipient, excluding the ultimate beneficiary (84.10); covered content = web content and mobile apps a recipient provides or makes available, directly or through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements (84.84(a)); compliance dates: 2027-05-11 for recipients with 15 or more employees, 2028-05-10 for fewer than 15 (84.84(b))
key_questions: Does the deploying organization receive HHS financial assistance (e.g. Medicare, Medicaid, grants)?; Does it have 15 or more employees?; Is the AI tool delivered as web content or a mobile app that the recipient provides directly or through a vendor contract?; Does the interface conform to WCAG 2.1 A and AA?; Does any 84.85 exception apply?
obligations: Make web content and mobile apps it provides, directly or through contractual or licensing arrangements, conform to WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA, unless it can show a fundamental alteration or undue financial and administrative burden.
enforcement: HHS OCR.
notes: Edge case: not AI-specific; included because patient-facing AI tools are web or mobile content. The extension is an interim final rule, so dates could change again.

title: Section 1557 nondiscrimination in patient care decision support tools
effective_date_notes: General prohibition in 92.210(a) applies from the rule's effective date, 2024-07-05. Duties to identify (b) and mitigate (c) risk apply within 300 days of 2024-07-05, i.e. 2025-05-01 (45 CFR 92.1 compliance table).
triggers: A covered entity uses a patient care decision support tool (including AI or algorithms) in its health programs or activities, particularly one with inputs measuring race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability.
example_tools: sepsis or deterioration early-warning score used by a hospital; race- or age-adjusted clinical equation (e.g. eGFR) or risk calculator; health plan utilization-review or prior-authorization algorithm affecting patient care; AI triage or care-management prioritization model; diagnostic imaging AI used by a clinic; non-automated triage flowchart (e.g. crisis standards of care)
exclusions: Applies only to section 1557 covered entities, not to developers as such: HHS states that ONC's Predictive DSI rule (HTI-1) applies to health IT developers while 92.210 applies to covered-entity users of patient care decision support tools, and a covered entity that develops its own tool may be subject to both (89 FR 37643). Does not apply to tools unrelated to clinical decision-making affecting patient care or outside the covered entity's health programs or activities; the preamble's examples, when unrelated to clinical decision-making affecting patient care, are tools for administrative and billing-related activities, automated medical coding, fraud, waste and abuse, patient scheduling, facilities management, inventory and materials management, supply chain management, financial market investment management, and employment and staffing-related activities (preamble discussion of 92.210). The (b) identification duty, and so the (c) mitigation duty, reach only tools whose input variables or factors measure race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability; the (a) prohibition covers discrimination through any patient care decision support tool.
key_definitions: 'Patient care decision support tool' = any automated or non-automated tool, mechanism, method, technology, or combination thereof used by a covered entity to support clinical decision-making in its health programs or activities (45 CFR 92.4); preamble: includes tools used by hospitals, providers, and payers for screening, risk prediction, diagnosis, prognosis, clinical decision-making, treatment planning, health care operations, and allocation of resources as applied to the patient, including tools to assess health status, recommend care, provide disease management guidance, determine eligibility, and conduct utilization review related to patient care that is directed by a provider (89 FR 37544-45); 'Covered entity' = a recipient of Federal financial assistance, HHS, or an ACA title I entity that administers a health program or activity (92.4); 'Federal financial assistance' = any grant, loan, credit, subsidy, contract (other than a procurement contract but including a contract of insurance), or other arrangement by which the Federal Government directly or indirectly provides funds, services of Federal personnel, or property, and includes HHS assistance such as advance payments of the premium tax credit, cost-sharing reduction payments, and payments or subsidies to entities providing health insurance coverage (92.4). The regulation text does not name Medicare Parts A-D. Preamble: entities that receive funding through Medicare Part C or Part D are subject to the rule as recipients of Federal financial assistance, including Medicare Advantage and Part D plans (and EGWPs), though employers and plan sponsors are not liable for their employment practices (89 FR 37619-20); the same document revises HHS's interpretation so that Medicare Part B constitutes Federal financial assistance (89 FR 37522, abstract).
key_questions: Is the user a 1557 covered entity (receives Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare Part A, B, C, or D, other HHS funds, or is a Marketplace issuer)?; Does the tool support clinical decision-making about patients (including utilization review), rather than billing, coding, scheduling, or staffing?; Do its inputs or factors measure race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability?; What has the covered entity done to identify such tools and mitigate discrimination risk?
obligations: Do not discriminate through these tools, make reasonable efforts to identify tools that use those input variables, and make reasonable efforts to mitigate the risk of discrimination.
enforcement: HHS Office for Civil Rights enforces through complaints and compliance reviews using the Title VI, Title IX, Section 504, and Age Discrimination Act mechanisms (45 CFR 92.301), up to suspension or termination of federal funding (92.303). HHS says courts recognize a private right of action under Section 1557; the rule governs only OCR's administrative enforcement (89 FR 37522 preamble). The rule sets no damages or civil money penalties.
notes: Verifier changed effective_date from 2025-05-01 to 2024-07-05 because 92.210(a) applies from the effective date; 2025-05-01 is the (b)-(c) compliance date. Section 92.210 is not among the provisions vacated in the 2026-06-02 notice. No HHS proposal to rescind it found.

title: CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F)
effective_date_notes: Rule effective 2024-04-08 (FR DATES). From 2026-01-01: specific denial reasons (for MA, 42 CFR 422.122(a)), 7-calendar-day standard decisions for items and services subject to prior authorization rules (422.568(b)(1)(ii)), public reporting, and Patient Access API metrics. From 2027-01-01: Prior Authorization API (422.122(b)), Provider Access and Payer-to-Payer APIs.
trigger_rule: utilization_review AND (org_plan OR org_developer) AND (plan_medicare_advantage OR plan_medicaid_chip OR plan_marketplace)
triggers: A Medicare Advantage organization, state Medicaid or CHIP agency or managed care plan, or Marketplace qualified health plan issuer runs prior authorization, including with automated or AI tools.
example_tools: AI prior-authorization decision engine for a Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care plan; automated denial-letter or denial-reason generator; FHIR Prior Authorization API product for payers; prior-authorization metrics reporting tool; payer-to-payer or provider-access data exchange service
exclusions: Applies only to impacted payers: MA organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges. Excludes issuers offering only stand-alone dental plans and QHP issuers offering only QHPs in the FF-SHOPs (89 FR 8758 preamble). Prior authorization provisions exclude drugs (e.g. 42 CFR 422.122(a), (b)(1)). Does not reach traditional Medicare fee-for-service or commercial plans outside these programs.
key_definitions: Denial reason duty: from 2026-01-01, an MA organization that denies a prior authorization request (excluding drugs) must include a specific reason for the denial, regardless of communication method (42 CFR 422.122(a)); Prior Authorization API: from 2027-01-01, a FHIR API listing items and services (excluding drugs) requiring prior authorization, required documentation, and request and response support (422.122(b)); MA prior authorization decision timeframes: 72 hours expedited, 7 calendar days standard (422.568, 422.572)
key_questions: Is the customer an MA organization, Medicaid or CHIP program or managed care plan, or FFE QHP issuer?; Does the tool make or support prior authorization decisions for items and services (not drugs)?; Does it generate the denial reason sent to providers?; Does it affect decision timeframes or public metrics?; Does the product implement the required FHIR APIs?; Do you run prior authorization yourself as a payer, or on a payer's behalf (the rule binds payers; providers and vendors are affected only through that role)?; Is the plan sold only on Covered California, a state-based exchange, where the Federally-facilitated Exchange QHP requirements may not reach?
obligations: Decide prior authorization requests within set timeframes (for MA: 72 hours expedited, 7 calendar days standard), give a specific reason for each denial, report prior authorization metrics publicly, and implement FHIR APIs from 2027.
enforcement: CMS oversight of MA, Medicaid, and QHP programs.
notes: MA dates and timeframes read in eCFR 422.122 and 422.568; rule effective date from FR DATES; other payer types follow parallel provisions (not each read). Not AI-specific; included because AI utilization-management tools sit inside this process.

title: CMS FAQ on Medicare Advantage coverage criteria and use of algorithms and AI
citation: CMS HPMS memo, Frequently Asked Questions related to Coverage Criteria and Utilization Management Requirements in CMS Final Rule (CMS-4201-F), 2024-02-06
effective_date_notes: Issued as a final FAQ memo dated 2024-02-06 (date confirmed in the memo itself). Explains rules applicable to coverage beginning 2024-01-01 under CMS-4201-F.
triggers: A Medicare Advantage organization uses algorithms or AI in coverage determinations.
example_tools: Medicare Advantage prior-authorization review AI; post-acute (SNF, home health, rehab) length-of-stay prediction tool used to decide when to end coverage; inpatient admission or observation-stay screening algorithm; tool that checks requests against a plan's publicly posted internal coverage criteria; utilization-management vendor platform used by an MA plan; automated denial-recommendation engine
exclusions: Guidance, not binding law (CMS FAQ memo dated 2024-02-06 to all Medicare Advantage organizations and Medicare-Medicaid Plans). Does not address traditional Medicare, Medicaid-only, or commercial plans. The memo does not ban algorithms or AI: a tool may assist coverage decisions if the MA organization still complies with 42 CFR 422.101(c) (Q2).
key_definitions: AI (quoting 15 U.S.C. 9401(3)) = 'a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments' (Q2); 'algorithm' is described as a decisional flow chart of if-then statements as well as predictive algorithms (Q2); 'publicly accessible' internal coverage criteria = reachable on a website (the plan's, or a delegated vendor's linked from the plan's), not behind a paywall or subscription, open to the public and not only enrollees or contracted providers (Q3); internal coverage criteria are allowed only when Traditional Medicare criteria are not fully established, and must rest on current evidence in widely used treatment guidelines or clinical literature (Q1, Q4); publicly posted criteria are 'static and unchanging', so AI cannot shift criteria over time or apply internal criteria that were not made public (Q2)
key_questions: Is the user a Medicare Advantage organization or Medicare-Medicaid Plan (or a vendor acting for one)?; Does the tool make or recommend coverage, admission, or termination-of-services decisions?; Does the decision rest on the individual enrollee's history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes, or on a larger data set or a prediction alone (e.g. predicted length of stay)?; Does the tool apply only criteria in Medicare statute, regulations, NCDs, LCDs, or publicly posted internal criteria?; Does a physician or appropriate professional review every expected adverse medical necessity decision?; Has the plan checked the tool for bias (Section 1557 reminder in Q2)?
obligations: CMS says plans may use algorithms or AI to assist coverage decisions, but each medical necessity decision must rest on the individual enrollee's circumstances, and algorithms may not change or deviate from publicly posted coverage criteria.
enforcement: CMS contract oversight.
notes: GUIDANCE, not binding law. Verified 2026-10-07 against the official memo PDF (HPMS_Memo_FAQ_on_CC_and_UM_020624.pdf, 14 pages) inside the cms.gov weekly HPMS archive zip for Feb 5-9, 2024 (https://www.cms.gov/files/zip/hpms-memos-wk-2-february-5-9-2024.zip); CMS does not post the memo as a standalone page, so primary_source_url is the archive page that links the zip. AI/algorithm content is in Q2; Section 1557 reminder in Q2; publicly accessible criteria in Q3.

title: CMS WISeR Model (technology-enabled prior authorization in traditional Medicare)
effective_date_notes: Model began 2026-01-01 for six performance years (through 2031-12-31) in New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington. Prior authorization requests accepted from 2026-01-05 for services on or after 2026-01-15; claims without a request are subject to pre-payment review for dates of service on or after 2026-01-15. Two services delayed until a date to be set in a later FR notice (91 FR 17282, effective 2026-04-06): deep brain stimulation for essential tremor and Parkinson's disease (NCD 160.24) and percutaneous image-guided lumbar decompression (NCD 150.13); no later notice found as of 2026-10-10.
triggers: A Medicare fee-for-service provider or supplier in a participating state furnishes a selected service (for example skin and tissue substitutes where an LCD applies); or a technology company serves as a model participant.
example_tools: AI-assisted prior-authorization review run by a CMS model participant for traditional Medicare; pre-payment medical-review automation for selected services; provider-side prior-authorization submission workflow for selected services; documentation-completeness checker for nerve-stimulator, epidural-injection, or skin-substitute requests; clinician-review queue with ML triage of requests
exclusions: Applies only to Medicare fee-for-service claims for the selected services furnished in the model states (New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, Washington); not Medicare Advantage (the notice treats MA as a comparison). Skin and tissue substitutes are selected only in MAC jurisdictions with an active LCD. Inpatient-only services and services that pose a substantial risk if delayed were screened out when services were chosen. The model does not change coverage, payment, or documentation requirements for the selected services. Submitting a prior authorization request is voluntary for providers (skipping it triggers pre-payment review). Two services are delayed until a later Federal Register notice: deep brain stimulation (NCD 160.24) and percutaneous image-guided lumbar decompression (NCD 150.13) (91 FR 17282).
key_definitions: WISeR = Wasteful and Inappropriate Services Reduction Model, a 6-year model in two 3-year agreement periods starting 2026-01-01 (90 FR 28750); 'model participants' = companies with experience implementing technology-enhanced prior authorization with other payers including MA plans, paid a share of averted expenditures (90 FR 28750-51); selected services from 2026-01-01 = electrical nerve stimulators (NCD 160.7), sacral nerve stimulation for urinary incontinence (NCD 230.18), phrenic nerve stimulator (160.19), deep brain stimulation for essential tremor and Parkinson's (160.24; delayed, see effective_date_notes), vagus nerve stimulation (160.18), induced lesions of nerve tracts (160.1), epidural steroid injections (excluding facet joint), percutaneous vertebral augmentation, cervical fusion, arthroscopic lavage and debridement for the osteoarthritic knee (150.9), hypoglossal nerve stimulation for OSA, incontinence control devices (230.10), diagnosis and treatment of impotence (230.4), percutaneous image-guided lumbar decompression (150.13; delayed), skin and tissue substitutes (LCD jurisdictions only) (90 FR 28751); 'provisional affirmation' = preliminary finding that a future claim likely meets Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements (90 FR 28752); model participants serve as HIPAA business associates of the Medicare FFS health plan and must sign BAAs (90 FR 28753)
key_questions: Is the provider or supplier enrolled in Medicare fee-for-service and located in NJ, OH, OK, TX, AZ, or WA?; Is the item or service on the selected-service list?; Is the tool run by (or sold to) a CMS model participant doing prior authorization or pre-payment review for the MAC?; Does a clinician review before a non-affirmation (notice says technology plus clinician review)?; Does the product touch PHI as a business associate of Medicare FFS?; Is the customer a Medicare Advantage plan (outside this model; see US-42CFR422.101)?
obligations: Providers and suppliers of selected services in the model states may submit a prior authorization request to the MAC or the model participant (voluntary); if they do not, the claim is subject to pre-payment medical review by the model participant, which may use technology and clinician review, and the MAC processes the claim per the participant's decision. A non-affirmed request gets a detailed reason and can be resubmitted without limit; a claim submitted after a non-affirmation is denied by the MAC with normal appeal rights. Model participants must comply with HIPAA as business associates.
enforcement: CMS Innovation Center model; payment denials.
notes: States, dates, review process read in the FR notices and the CMS FAQ (2026-10-10). Verifier removed health_plan from applies_to (traditional Medicare, no plans) and added health_facility. Congressional Review Act resolutions (H.J.Res. 187, S.J.Res. 192, S.J.Res. 198) were introduced in May-June 2026; none passed, and the Senate rejected a motion to proceed on S.J.Res. 198, 46-50, on 2026-07-16 (govinfo BILLSTATUS). The model remains in effect. GAO's view that the notice is a rule comes from a secondary source only.

title: FTC COPPA Rule amendments (2025)
effective_date_notes: Amended rule effective 2025-06-23; operators must comply by 2026-04-22, except 312.11(d)(1), (d)(4), and (g) (safe harbor provisions), which apply from 2025-06-23 (FR DATES).
triggers: An online service or app is directed to children under 13, or knowingly collects personal data from them, including health and wellness apps and chatbots.
example_tools: AI homework or health-education chatbot aimed at children under 13; pediatric symptom checker app directed at kids; children's mindfulness or mental-wellness app; kids' fitness or sleep tracker; voice-AI toy or game that records children; family health app that knows some users are under 13
exclusions: Protects only children under 13 ('child' = under 13, 16 CFR 312.2); teens 13 and older are not covered. Applies to operators of commercial websites or online services directed to children, or operators with actual knowledge they collect personal information from a child (312.3). A mixed-audience service is not deemed directed to children for visitors not identified as under 13 (312.2). A service is not directed to children solely because it links to a child-directed service (312.2). Nonprofit entities that would be exempt from FTC Act section 5 are not 'operators' (312.2). Support for internal operations (e.g. security, contextual ads, personalization) is carved out of 'disclose' (312.2). The definitions and general provisions read (312.2, 312.3) contain no HIPAA carve-out; other sections not checked.
key_definitions: 'Child' = under 13 (312.2); 'personal information' = individually identifiable information collected online, including name, address, online contact information, screen or user name that works as contact information, telephone number, government identifier, persistent identifier (cookie ID, IP address, device serial or unique device identifier), photo, video, or audio file containing a child's image or voice, geolocation sufficient to identify street and city, biometric identifier (fingerprints, retina or iris patterns, genetic data, voiceprints, gait, faceprints), and other information combined with those (312.2); 'operator' = person operating a website or online service for commercial purposes that collects or maintains personal information from users, or on whose behalf it is collected (312.2); 'directed to children' = commercial website or online service targeted to children, judged by subject matter, visuals, animated characters, music, models, language, advertising, and empirical audience evidence; also deemed directed if it has actual knowledge it collects from users of a child-directed service (312.2); 'obtaining verifiable consent' = reasonable effort to ensure the parent receives notice and authorizes collection, use, and disclosure (312.2); operator duties = notice (312.4), verifiable parental consent before collection, use, or disclosure (312.5), parental review and refusal (312.6), no conditioning participation on excess data (312.7), reasonable security (312.8) (312.3)
key_questions: Are any users under 13?; Is the app or chatbot directed to children (content, characters, marketing) or do you have actual knowledge that a user is under 13?; Do you collect voice recordings, photos, persistent identifiers, geolocation, or biometrics from them?; Do you disclose child data to third parties (ad networks, analytics, model vendors)?; Do you age-screen neutrally (mixed audience)?; Are you a nonprofit outside FTC Act section 5?
obligations: Get verifiable parental consent, give parents the option to consent to collection without consenting to disclosure to third parties (separate consent for non-integral disclosures), and keep children's data only as long as reasonably necessary, then delete it.
enforcement: FTC civil penalties.
notes: Edge-case inclusion: general privacy rule reaching child-directed health AI tools. Read in eCFR 312.5 and 312.10. Verifier removed "(including for AI training)" from obligations: not found in the rule text searched. effective_date kept at 2025-06-23 (safe harbor duties apply then); most operator duties start 2026-04-22.

Agency actions taken under it may persist until suspended, revised, or rescinded (outcome not checked).

title: EO 14179 Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
effective_date_notes: Signed 2025-01-23; published 2025-01-31 (FR API).
triggers: Sets federal policy on AI development; directs review of actions taken under the revoked EO 14110.
example_tools: No private tool is directly regulated. Signal for: federal agency AI procurement and use policy (OMB M-24-10 and M-24-18 as revised); HHS and other agency deregulatory proposals citing the order (e.g. ONC HTI-5); health AI vendors selling to federal agencies
exclusions: Creates no rights or duties enforceable by any party (section 6(c)); implemented consistent with applicable law and appropriations (6(b)); does not impair agency authority or OMB functions (6(a)). Does not itself rescind any specific rule; it directs agencies to review and, as appropriate and consistent with law, suspend, revise, or rescind actions taken under revoked EO 14110 (section 5(a)).

enforcement: None directly.
notes: Executive order, not law that binds private parties. Text read in FR. Verifier changed effective_date from 2025-01-31 (publication) to 2025-01-23 (signing), matching the other EO rows. ONC's HTI-5 proposal cites this order as a reason to remove DSI transparency requirements.

title: EO 14365 Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence
effective_date_notes: Signed 2025-12-11; published 2025-12-16 (FR API). Most directives ran on 30 and 90 day clocks.
triggers: Targets state AI laws seen as onerous, including those that could affect health AI tools.
example_tools: Health AI tool sold across several states whose developer faces state AI laws (clinical decision support, patient chatbot, utilization-review model); AI developer subject to Colorado-style algorithmic discrimination rules; AI vendor subject to state AI disclosure or reporting laws; state agency applying for federal broadband or discretionary grants
exclusions: Directs federal agencies; does not itself preempt state law or bind private parties (section 9(c) creates no enforceable rights). The legislative recommendation it calls for shall not propose preempting otherwise lawful state AI laws on child safety protections, AI compute and data center infrastructure (other than generally applicable permitting reforms), or state government procurement and use of AI (section 8(b)). Implementation status as of 2026-10-10 is in notes (DOJ task force and one intervention; FTC statement proposed only; no Commerce list or FCC proceeding found).
key_definitions: AI Litigation Task Force (DOJ, within 30 days) to challenge state AI laws inconsistent with the policy, including on interstate commerce, preemption by federal regulations, or other grounds (section 3); Commerce evaluation within 90 days identifying onerous state AI laws, at minimum those that 'require AI models to alter their truthful outputs' or compel disclosure or reporting that would violate the First Amendment (section 4); states with identified laws ineligible for BEAD non-deployment funds to the maximum extent allowed (section 5(a)); agencies to assess conditioning discretionary grants on states not enacting or enforcing conflicting AI laws (section 5(b)); FCC to start a proceeding on a federal reporting and disclosure standard for AI models that preempts conflicting state laws (section 6); FTC policy statement on when state laws requiring alterations to truthful AI outputs are preempted by FTC Act section 5 (section 7)
key_questions: Does the company operate in states with AI-specific laws (e.g. Colorado, California)?; Do those laws require altering model outputs or AI disclosures or reporting?; Is the user a state relying on BEAD or federal discretionary grant funding?; Has DOJ or Commerce identified the specific state law?; Is the question about child-safety AI laws (carved out of the recommended preemption)?
obligations: Directs DOJ to form an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws, Commerce to publish within 90 days an evaluation identifying onerous state AI laws and set BEAD funding conditions, agencies to consider conditioning discretionary grants, the FCC to consider a preemptive federal AI disclosure standard, and the FTC to issue a Section 5 policy statement on state laws that require altering truthful AI outputs. It does not itself preempt state law.
enforcement: DOJ litigation against states; funding conditions.
notes: Executive order; directs agencies, does not itself preempt state law or create rights (Sec. 9(c)). Text read in FR. Implementation as of 2026-10-10: DOJ AI Litigation Task Force created by AG memo dated 2026-01-09; DOJ moved to intervene (2026-04-24) in xAI's suit against Colorado SB24-205; FTC published a proposed (not final) policy statement (91 FR 41638, 2026-07-07); White House legislative recommendations issued March 2026. Not found: the Commerce evaluation of state AI laws, the NTIA BEAD notice, and an FCC preemptive disclosure-standard proceeding.

title: FCC NPRM on AI-generated calls and texts
effective_date_notes: Comments were due 2024-10-10 and replies 2024-10-25 (FR DATES). No order, further notice, or withdrawal found in the Federal Register through 2026-10-10; the FCC's 2026 Unified Agenda entry (91 FR 53092) lists the next action as undetermined.
triggers: Would apply to callers and texters using AI-generated voice or content in outbound calls and autodialed texts.
example_tools: AI voice agent that places appointment-reminder calls; AI outbound care-outreach caller (refill, care-gap, wellness calls); autodialed text campaigns with AI-generated content; voice-cloned clinician message; AI scheduling agent that places calls; AI speech tool used by a person with a speech or hearing disability to make calls
exclusions: Not in force (proposed); signal only. Per the NPRM the proposed definition focuses on outbound calls, and TCPA requirements 'do not extend to technologies used to answer inbound calls' (89 FR 73322, para. 3). Text disclosure would apply only to autodialed texts that meet the ATDS definition and the AI-generated definition. Proposed exemption from TCPA consent and identification rules for artificial or prerecorded voice calls made by individuals with speech or hearing disabilities using AI or other technology to communicate, so long as the call carries no unsolicited advertisement or telemarketing (paras. 10-18).
key_definitions: Proposed 'AI generated call' = 'a call that uses any technology or tool to generate an artificial or prerecorded voice or a text using computational technology or other machine learning, including predictive algorithms, and large language models, to process natural language and produce voice or text content to communicate with a called party over an outbound telephone call' (para. 2); proposed disclosures = (1) in consent requests, that consent to artificial or prerecorded calls may include AI-generated calls, (2) same for autodialed texts with AI-generated content, (3) a clear disclosure at the start of each AI-generated voice call (para. 6); for calls needing prior express written consent, the written agreement would disclose authorization of AI-generated content
key_questions: Does the AI place outbound calls or send autodialed texts (versus answering inbound calls)?; Does it use synthetic or cloned voice, or LLM-generated voice or text content?; Does current consent language mention AI-generated content?; Would the call open with a clear AI disclosure?; Is the caller an individual with a speech or hearing disability using AI to communicate?; Has the FCC finalized this proposal (none found)?
obligations: Would define AI-generated calls, require callers to disclose AI use at the start of each AI-generated voice call and in consent requests for AI-generated calls and texts, and protect AI uses that help people with disabilities use the phone network. Not in force.
enforcement: FCC if finalized.
notes: PROPOSED, not in force. Read in FR text. Later FCC robocall proposals (90 FR 56101, 2025-12-05; 91 FR 57454, 2026-09-09) do not act on this docket; the 2025 notice mentions AI only in passing questions (read 2026-10-10), the 2026 notice was seen by title only.

title: FCC Declaratory Ruling: AI-generated voices are artificial voices under TCPA
effective_date_notes: Adopted 2024-02-02; released 2024-02-08 (ruling text).
triggers: A caller uses AI technology that generates human voices (voice cloning or synthetic voice) in an outbound call.
example_tools: AI voice agent for appointment reminders; AI outbound care-outreach or refill-reminder caller; voice-cloned clinician or health plan message; text-to-speech notification calls to patients; AI-voiced health survey or enrollment calls; AI-generated voicemail drops
exclusions: Does not ban AI voice calls; it requires the consent the TCPA already requires (emergency purpose or an exemption excepted) (FCC 24-17 paras. 2, 5, 9). FCC exemptions are unchanged (47 CFR 64.1200(a)(3), (9), per n.4). A call that delivers a 'health care' message by or on behalf of a HIPAA covered entity or business associate is carved out of the prior express written consent rule for advertising and telemarketing calls (47 CFR 64.1200(a)(2)); ordinary prior express consent for artificial or prerecorded voice calls still applies per the ruling. The ruling concerns calls made or initiated using an artificial or prerecorded voice; a live human speaking without an autodialer or artificial voice is not addressed. The separate 2024 NPRM states TCPA requirements do not extend to technology used to answer inbound calls (not part of this ruling).
key_definitions: 'Artificial or prerecorded voice' under the TCPA encompasses 'current AI technologies that resemble human voices and/or generate call content using a prerecorded voice' (para. 5); voice cloning is included because the technology 'artificially simulates a human voice' and a person is not speaking (para. 5); a live agent selecting prerecorded or AI messages does not negate that the call is initiated using an artificial or prerecorded voice (para. 8, Soundboard Ruling); prior express written consent is required where the call includes or introduces an advertisement or is telemarketing (para. 5 n.13, para. 9); all artificial or prerecorded messages must state at the start the identity of the business or entity responsible for initiating the call (47 CFR 64.1200(b)(1), quoted at n.23)
key_questions: Is the call outbound and made with a synthetic, cloned, or AI-generated voice?; Do you hold the called party's prior express consent (written if the call advertises or is telemarketing)?; Is it an emergency-purpose call or a health care message by a covered entity or business associate?; Does the message identify the responsible entity at the start?; Is the voice AI-generated or is a live person speaking?
obligations: Calls using AI-generated voices are artificial or prerecorded voice calls under the TCPA: they need the called party's prior express consent absent an emergency purpose or exemption, must give the identification and disclosure information FCC rules require, and, for telemarketing, must offer opt-out methods. Not banned.
enforcement: FCC enforcement; private TCPA suits.
notes: Ruling text read (docs.fcc.gov PDF); the fcc.gov news page returned 403. Primary URL replaced the guessed fcc.gov page. instrument_type kept as `regulation`; a declaratory ruling interprets the statute (judgment call). The 2024 NPRM confirms the Commission had already determined voice cloning is an artificial voice.

title: FDA draft guidance: AI-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations
effective_date_notes: FR notice of availability 2025-01-07; fda.gov lists it as draft (January 2025) on 2026-10-07. No final version found.
triggers: A company seeks FDA marketing authorization for a device with AI-enabled software functions.
example_tools: AI radiology triage or CAD software preparing a 510(k); ML sepsis or deterioration predictor seeking De Novo authorization; AI ECG analysis software; deep-learning skin lesion classifier; LLM-based clinical software function submitted as a device; AI insulin-dosing software
exclusions: Not in force (draft guidance, 'Draft - Not for Implementation', non-binding); signal only. Covers only 'device software functions' (software that meets the device definition in FD&C Act 201(h)); software excluded by section 520(o), such as qualifying non-device CDS or general wellness software, is outside. Recommendations are for marketing submissions (510(k), De Novo, PMA, HDE, BLA; some may apply to IDE). Not a complete list of submission content (Section II).
key_definitions: 'AI-enabled device' = a device including one or more AI-enabled device software functions (AI-DSFs); 'AI-DSF' = a device software function that implements one or more AI models; 'model' = a mathematical construct that generates an inference or prediction based on new input data (Section II); 'marketing submission' = 510(k), De Novo, PMA, HDE, or BLA (Section II); an AI-enabled device can be substantially equivalent to a non-AI device with the same intended use if it raises no different questions of safety and effectiveness (Section II); 'validation' follows 21 CFR 820.3(z) and should not be used for training or tuning (Section IV); 'development' = training, tuning, and tuning evaluation; 'test data' used for verification and validation (Section IV); transparency and bias addressed across the total product life cycle (Section III)
key_questions: Is the software function a device under FD&C 201(h), or excluded under 520(o)?; Is a marketing submission (510(k), De Novo, PMA) planned?; Does it use an ML or AI model?; Do you have plans for bias and representativeness testing and for performance monitoring after release?; Will you propose a predetermined change control plan (see US-FDA-PCCP-GUIDANCE)?
obligations: Would recommend what a submission contains: device description, user interface and labeling (transparency), risk assessment, data management, model description and development, validation, performance monitoring, cybersecurity, and a public submission summary. Draft only.
enforcement: FDA premarket review.
notes: DRAFT guidance, non-binding, not for implementation. Content checked against the draft's table of contents (fda.gov/media/184856/download).

title: FDA classification of radiological computer-assisted detection and diagnosis software
effective_date_notes: Final order effective 2025-06-13; the classification was applicable from 2018-05-24 (FR DATES). A petition to exempt this and related radiology CAD/CADt types from 510(k) was denied (final order 91 FR 58817, effective 2026-09-17), so 510(k) is still required.
triggers: Software that detects, localizes, or characterizes findings on medical images (for example fractures or lesions) to inform diagnostic and patient management decisions.
example_tools: chest X-ray nodule detection AI; mammography CADe/CADx software; fracture detection AI on radiographs; CT lesion characterization software; MRI finding detection and localization AI; stroke or hemorrhage image-analysis software
exclusions: Covers image processing software that detects, localizes, and characterizes findings on acquired medical images (radiography, MR, CT) and informs the clinical user's diagnostic and patient management decisions (21 CFR 892.2090(a)). The device is not a replacement for complete clinician review or judgment (892.2090(a)). Image software that only produces quantitative outputs (segmentation, landmarking, view selection) with a PCCP is classified separately at 892.2055 (see US-FDA-MLQI-2026). Software that does not analyze medical images is outside this classification.
key_definitions: 'Radiological computer-assisted detection and diagnostic software' = 'an image processing device intended to aid in the detection, localization, and characterization of fracture, lesions, or other disease-specific findings on acquired medical images (e.g., radiography, magnetic resonance, computed tomography)'; it detects, identifies, and characterizes findings from features extracted from images and gives the user information on presence, location, and characteristics; the analysis is 'intended to inform the primary diagnostic and patient management decisions that are made by the clinical user' (892.2090(a)); special controls = algorithm description, pre-specified standalone and reader-study testing, software documentation including hazard analysis and cybersecurity, and labeling on population, instructions, user, inputs and outputs, compatible hardware, limitations, performance summary (892.2090(b))
key_questions: Does your intended use match this classification's identification exactly? (If not, this classification does not apply, but another device pathway may.); Does the software analyze acquired medical images (X-ray, CT, MR)?; Does it detect, localize, or characterize findings?; Is the output meant to inform the clinician's primary diagnostic decision?; Is there a 510(k) with a predicate under this classification?; Do you have standalone and reader-study performance data across relevant subgroups and equipment?
obligations: Class II (special controls), 510(k) required. Special controls include design verification and validation with a detailed algorithm description (inputs, outputs, limitations), pre-specified performance testing (standalone and, as applicable, side-by-side or reader studies), and the other controls in 892.2090(b).
enforcement: FDA premarket and postmarket enforcement.
notes: Classification order (De Novo codification), read in FR and eCFR. Labeling controls not read in full.

title: FDA Clinical Decision Support Software guidance (revised 2026)
effective_date_notes: Current version issued 2026-01-29 and supersedes a version issued 2026-01-06 (guidance PDF front page), which replaced the 2022 CDS guidance. No FR notice of availability found.
triggers: Software analyzes patient-specific medical information and gives recommendations, alerts, or outputs on prevention, diagnosis, or treatment, and the developer must decide whether it is a regulated device or 'Non-Device CDS' under FD&C 520(o)(1)(E). The CDS exclusion is available only for software intended for health care professionals; software for patients or caregivers is a device under this guidance. Image, IVD-signal, and pattern or signal inputs, specific diagnostic or treatment directives, and time-critical alarms keep software a device.
example_tools: drug-drug and drug-allergy interaction alerts in an EHR; evidence-based order sets for clinicians; guideline-matching tool that lists treatment options for a clinician; differential-diagnosis support for clinicians; sepsis or stroke early-warning alert (device under this guidance); consumer symptom-checker or triage app for patients (not covered by the CDS exclusion)
exclusions: Guidance is non-binding. It covers only the 520(o)(1)(E) exclusion for CDS intended for health care professionals (HCPs; licensed, registered, or certified to administer health care, n.1). Software that supports or provides recommendations to patients or caregivers, not HCPs, cannot use the 520(o)(1)(E) exclusion; FDA states such software 'meet[s] the definition of a device' and says it will follow existing policies (device software and mobile medical apps, General Wellness, and others) for non-HCP CDS (Section IV(3)). Inference: whether a particular patient-facing function is regulated still depends on its intended use and those other policies and exclusions. Stays a device: software intended to acquire, process, or analyze a medical image, an IVD signal, or a pattern or signal from a signal acquisition system (Criterion 1); software giving a specific preventive, diagnostic, or treatment output or directive (Criterion 3); software for a critical, time-sensitive task or decision (Criterion 4(a)). Time-critical alerts: example V.C.11 says software that analyzes patient-specific information to detect a life-threatening condition such as stroke or sepsis and generate an alarm or alert to an HCP is a device ('does not meet Criterion 3 or 4... supports time-critical decision-making'); similar device examples cover MI identification from ECG and enzymes (22), heart-failure hospitalization prediction (23), deterioration alerts from hourly pulse oximetry and heart rate in the EHR (24), CGM hypoglycemia detection every 30 minutes (25), stroke triage (26-27), and patient insulin dosing (28). Single recommendation: where only one option is clinically appropriate and the function otherwise meets all criteria, FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion (Section IV(3)), but not for examples such as a 24-hour cardiovascular event prediction, near-real-time physiologic mortality prediction that guides immediate escalation, acute or emergent back pain pathways, or functions using images, genomic data, or unverifiable sources. The guidance does not address other FD&C requirements for device software or labeling of drug or biologic decision support (Section III).
key_definitions: All four criteria must be met (Section IV): (1) 'not intended to acquire, process, or analyze a medical image or a signal from an in vitro diagnostic device or a pattern or signal from a signal acquisition system'; (2) intended for 'displaying, analyzing, or printing medical information about a patient or other medical information (such as peer-reviewed clinical studies and clinical practice guidelines)' (520(o)(1)(E)(i)); (3) intended for 'supporting or providing recommendations to a health care professional about prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of a disease or condition' (520(o)(1)(E)(ii)); (4) intended for 'enabling such health care professional to independently review the basis for such recommendations... so that it is not the intent that such health care professional rely primarily on any of such recommendations' (520(o)(1)(E)(iii)). Signal and pattern: 'pattern' = multiple, sequential, or repeated measurements of a signal or from a signal acquisition system; discrete, episodic, or intermittent point-in-time physiological measurements (e.g. routine vital signs at discrete clinical encounters) generally do not by themselves constitute a pattern (IV(1)); a single, discrete, clinically meaningful test result (e.g. a blood glucose lab result) is medical information, while continuous sampling (e.g. CGM readings) is a pattern or signal (IV(2)); a lab result in an EHR is listed as medical information (IV(2)), but hourly pulse oximetry and heart rate from an EHR analyzed for deterioration were treated as a pattern (V.C.24). Criterion 3 = condition-, disease-, or patient-specific recommendations to an HCP that enhance, inform, or influence a decision, without a specific output or directive and without replacing the HCP's judgment; lists, prioritized lists, and follow-up options qualify (IV(3)). Criterion 4 recommendations = intended use, HCP user, and patient population stated and use not time-critical; required inputs identified with plain-language instructions; plain-language description of algorithm development and validation (approach such as AI/ML, data representativeness, validation results); output showing patient-specific information and knowns/unknowns; FDA weighs level of automation and time-critical nature, citing automation bias (IV(4)).
key_questions: Is the intended user a licensed HCP, or a patient or caregiver?; Does the software analyze medical images, IVD signals, or continuous or serial signals (ECG, CGM, wearable streams, repeated vitals)?; Or does it use only discrete patient data (diagnosis, symptoms, single lab values, routine vitals at encounters) and clinical guidelines?; Does it give a specific diagnosis or treatment directive or an alert or alarm, or a list or prioritized options for the HCP to consider?; Is the decision time-critical (sepsis, stroke, MI, deterioration, 24-hour risk)?; Can the HCP see the inputs, the logic, and the validation in plain language?; Is only one option clinically appropriate (possible enforcement discretion)?
obligations: Explains which CDS functions meet the 520(o)(1)(E) exclusion; recommends that the software or labeling identify required inputs and give a plain-language description of the algorithm's development, validation, and data so an HCP can independently review the basis; and says FDA intends to exercise enforcement discretion for functions that meet the criteria but give a single clinically appropriate recommendation.
enforcement: FDA enforcement of device requirements.
notes: GUIDANCE, not binding law. Verifier changed signed and effective dates from 2026-01-06 to 2026-01-29 after reading the PDF (fda.gov/media/109618/download). Content read in the PDF.

title: FDA classification of cardiovascular machine learning-based notification software
effective_date_notes: Final order effective 2026-09-11; the classification was applicable from 2023-08-03 (FR DATES).
triggers: Machine learning software that uses non-invasive physiological inputs from routine care to suggest the likelihood of a single cardiovascular disease or condition for referral or diagnostic follow-up (not arrhythmia detection).
example_tools: ML screening notification for a single cardiovascular condition from routine vitals or ECG-type inputs; wearable-based cardiovascular risk notification that suggests referral (not arrhythmia); AI that flags likelihood of heart failure or cardiac disease from non-invasive sensor data for follow-up testing; ML notification software inside a patient monitoring platform
exclusions: Excludes software intended to identify or detect arrhythmias (21 CFR 870.2380(a)). Covers software that identifies a single condition, from one or more non-invasive physiological inputs obtained as part of routine medical care; it is a basis for further testing and not intended to provide diagnostic quality output. Multi-condition or diagnostic-quality software is not described by this identification (other pathways not stated in the text).
key_definitions: 'Cardiovascular machine learning-based notification software' = software that 'employs machine learning techniques to suggest the likelihood of a cardiovascular disease or condition for further referral or diagnostic follow-up'; it 'identifies a single condition based on one or more non-invasive physiological inputs as part of routine medical care', 'is intended as the basis for further testing and is not intended to provide diagnostic quality output', and 'is not intended to identify or detect arrhythmias' (870.2380(a)); special controls include clinical validation on an independent real-world test set from at least three geographically diverse sites separate from training sites, with subgroup performance and adjudicated ground truth (870.2380(b)(1)); software verification, validation, and hazard analysis; human factors assessment of misinterpretation risk (b)(3); labeling with a warning not to rely on absence of a finding to rule out follow-up and that output is not a substitute for full clinical evaluation (b)(4)
key_questions: Does your intended use match this classification's identification exactly? (If not, this classification does not apply, but another device pathway may.); Does the ML software suggest likelihood of one cardiovascular condition for referral or follow-up?; Are inputs non-invasive physiological signals from routine care?; Does it detect arrhythmias (excluded)?; Does it claim diagnostic-quality output (outside the identification)?; Do you have independent validation across three or more geographically diverse sites?
obligations: Class II (special controls). Special controls include clinical validation on an independent, representative real-world test dataset with subgroup performance estimates and adjudicated ground truth, justified performance goals, objective performance measures, and the other controls in 870.2380(b).
enforcement: FDA premarket and postmarket enforcement.
notes: Read in FR order and eCFR 870.2380. Verifier removed diagnostics_imaging from tool_categories (inputs are physiological signals, not images).

title: FDA General Wellness: Policy for Low Risk Devices (revised 2026)
effective_date_notes: Issued 2026-01-06; supersedes the version issued 2019-09-27 (guidance PDF front page).
trigger_rule: org_consumer_business AND (consumer_health_data OR neural_data OR mental_health_use)
triggers: A consumer wellness product or app (including wearables and AI coaching) whose intended use is only general wellness (stress, sleep, fitness, weight, mental acuity, or lifestyle choices that may help reduce risk of or help living well with named chronic diseases) and which is low risk (non-invasive, not implanted, no radiation or laser). Claims to diagnose, treat, screen, monitor, or manage a disease or condition (for example 'helps treat an anxiety disorder'), disease thresholds, or clinical-action alerts take the product outside the policy.
example_tools: fitness and activity tracker app; sleep-tracking app; stress, relaxation, or breathing-coach app; food-logging and weight-management app; wellness wearable showing heart rate, HRV, or blood pressure trends for wellness only; mindfulness app without disease claims
exclusions: Non-binding enforcement policy. Does not apply to products regulated by other FDA Centers (drugs, biologics, dietary supplements, foods, cosmetics) or to combination products (Section I). Outside the policy when intended uses go beyond general wellness (Section III) or the product is not low risk: invasive (penetrates or pierces skin or mucous membranes), implanted, or involving technology that could pose safety risk without regulatory controls such as lasers, radiation, or neurostimulation (Section IV).
